claim: Myelin ensheathment of axons enables rapid impulse propagation, which is a prerequisite for normal motor and sensory capabilities of vertebrates.
source: The ensheathment of axons with myelin enables rapid impulse propagation, a prerequisite for normal motor and sensory capabilities of vertebrates (Weil et al., 2018; Hartline and Colman, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weil et al., 2018 and Hartline and Colman, 2007

claim: Mutations affecting myelin genes MPZ, PMP22, GJB1 and PRX impair myelin integrity and reduce nerve conduction velocity in demyelinating neuropathies of the Charcot-Marie-Tooth spectrum.
source: This is illustrated by demyelinating neuropathies of the Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) spectrum, in which mutations affecting myelin genes as MPZ, PMP22, GJB1 and PRX impair myelin integrity and reduce the velocity of nerve conduction in the peripheral nervous system (PNS) (Rossor et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rossor et al., 2013

claim: Myelination by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves is regulated by axonal neuregulin-1.
source: Developmentally, myelination by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves is regulated by axonal neuregulin-1 (Michailov et al., 2004; Taveggia et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Michailov et al., 2004 and Taveggia et al., 2005

claim: Myelination by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves is regulated by the basal lamina.
source: Developmentally, myelination by Schwann cells in peripheral nerves is regulated by axonal neuregulin-1 (Michailov et al., 2004; Taveggia et al., 2005) and the basal lamina (Chernousov et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2015; Ghidinelli et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Chernousov et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2015; Ghidinelli et al., 2017

claim: The basal lamina is molecularly linked to the abaxonal Schwann cell membrane via integrins and the dystroglycan complex.
source: the basal lamina (Chernousov et al., 2008; Petersen et al., 2015; Ghidinelli et al., 2017) that is molecularly linked to the abaxonal Schwann cell membrane via integrins and the dystroglycan complex (Sherman et al., 2001; Masaki et al., 2002; Nodari et al., 2008; Raasakka et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sherman et al., 2001; Masaki et al., 2002; Nodari et al., 2008; Raasakka et al., 2019

claim: In adulthood, the basal lamina continues to enclose all axon/myelin-units.
source: In adulthood, the basal lamina continues to enclose all axon/myelin-units (Hess and Lansing, 1953), probably to maintain myelin.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hess and Lansing, 1953

claim: The Ig-domain containing myelin protein zero (MPZ; also termed P0) mediates adhesion between adjacent extracellular membrane surfaces in compact myelin.
source: For example, the Ig-domain containing myelin protein zero (MPZ; also termed P0) mediates adhesion between adjacent extracellular membrane surfaces in compact myelin (Giese et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giese et al., 1992

claim: At their intracellular surfaces, myelin membranes are compacted by the cytosolic domain of MPZ/P0 together with myelin basic protein (MBP).
source: At their intracellular surfaces, myelin membranes are compacted by the cytosolic domain of MPZ/P0 together with myelin basic protein (MBP; previously termed P1) (Martini et al., 1995; Nawaz et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martini et al., 1995; Nawaz et al., 2013

claim: MPZ/P0 and MBP were early identified as the most abundant peripheral myelin proteins.
source: Not surprisingly, MPZ/P0 and MBP were early identified as the most abundant peripheral myelin proteins (Greenfield et al., 1973; Brostoff et al., 1975).
evidence: Supported by citations to Greenfield et al., 1973; Brostoff et al., 1975

claim: A system of cytoplasmic channels through the otherwise compacted myelin sheath remains non-compacted throughout life, including the adaxonal myelin layer, paranodal loops, Schmidt-Lanterman incisures (SLI), and abaxonal longitudinal and transverse bands of cytoplasm termed bands of Cajal.
source: A system of cytoplasmic channels through the otherwise compacted myelin sheath remains non-compacted throughout life, that is the adaxonal myelin layer, paranodal loops, Schmidt-Lanterman incisures (SLI), and abaxonal longitudinal and transverse bands of cytoplasm termed bands of Cajal (Sherman and Brophy, 2005; Nave and Werner, 2014; Kleopa and Sargiannidou, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sherman and Brophy, 2005; Nave and Werner, 2014; Kleopa and Sargiannidou, 2015

claim: The cytosolic channels in myelin probably represent transport routes toward Schwann cell-dependent metabolic support of myelinated axons.
source: The cytosolic channels probably also represent transport routes toward Schwann cell-dependent metabolic support of myelinated axons (Court et al., 2004; Beirowski et al., 2014; Domènech-Estévez et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Gonçalves et al., 2017; Stassart et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Court et al., 2004; Beirowski et al., 2014; Domènech-Estévez et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Gonçalves et al., 2017; Stassart et al., 2018

claim: Oligonucleotide microarray analyses have been used for mRNA abundance profiling of total sciatic nerves.
source: Considering that Schwann cells constitute a major proportion of the cells in the PNS, oligonucleotide microarray analyses have been used for mRNA abundance profiling of total sciatic nerves (Nagarajan et al., 2002; Le et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nagarajan et al., 2002; Le et al., 2005

claim: Systematic microarray approaches allowed the identification of novel myelin constituents including non-compact myelin-associated protein (NCMAP/MP11).
source: Indeed, these systematic approaches allowed the identification of novel myelin constituents including non-compact myelin-associated protein (NCMAP/MP11) (Ryu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ryu et al., 2008

claim: Biochemically purified peripheral myelin is enriched for compact myelin markers (MPZ/P0, MBP, PMP2) and non-compact myelin markers (PRX) compared to nerve lysates.
source: By immunoblotting, proteins specific for both compact (MPZ/P0, MBP, PMP2) and non-compact (PRX) myelin were substantially enriched in the myelin fraction compared to nerve lysates (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Axonal (NEFH, KCNA1) and mitochondrial (VDAC) proteins and a marker for the Schwann cell nucleus (KROX20/EGR2) are strongly reduced in purified myelin compared to nerve lysates.
source: Conversely, axonal (NEFH, KCNA1) and mitochondrial (VDAC) proteins and a marker for the Schwann cell nucleus (KROX20/EGR2) were strongly reduced in purified myelin.
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 1B

claim: MSE data acquisition mode quantified 351 proteins in PNS myelin with a false discovery rate (FDR) of <1% at peptide and protein level and an average sequence coverage of 35.5%.
source: When applying the MSE mode to PNS myelin, we quantified 351 proteins with a false discovery rate (FDR) of <1% at peptide and protein level and an average sequence coverage of 35.5% (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—source data 1

claim: MSE data acquisition mode provides a dynamic range of more than four orders of magnitude for quantifying myelin proteins.
source: While MSE (labeled in orange in Figure 1C) indeed provided a dynamic range of more than four orders of magnitude and thus quantitatively covered the exceptionally abundant myelin proteins MPZ/P0, MBP and PRX
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C

claim: UDMSE data acquisition mode quantified 1078 proteins in PNS myelin with an average sequence coverage of 34.3%.
source: Accordingly, by using the UDMSE mode, which comprises ion mobility for additional peptide separation as well as drift time-specific collision energies for peptide fragmentation, proteome coverage was increased about three-fold (1078 proteins quantified; average sequence coverage 34.3%; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—source data 1

claim: DRE-UDMSE data acquisition mode quantified 554 proteins in PNS myelin with an average sequence coverage of 30.6%.
source: Indeed, DRE-UDMSE quantified an intermediate number of proteins in PNS myelin (554 proteins; average sequence coverage 30.6%; Figure 1—source data 1)
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—source data 1

claim: There is high reproducibility between replicates and among different data acquisition modes with Pearson's correlation coefficients for protein abundance in the range of 0.765–0.997.
source: Overall, we found a high reproducibility between replicates and even among the different data acquisition modes as indicated by Pearson's correlation coefficients for protein abundance in the range of 0.765–0.997 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The most abundant PNS myelin protein, myelin protein zero (MPZ/P0), constitutes 44% (+/- 4% relative standard deviation) of the total myelin protein.
source: According to quantitative assessment of this dataset, the most abundant PNS myelin protein, myelin protein zero (MPZ/P0), constitutes 44% (+/- 4% relative standard deviation (RSD)) of the total myelin protein (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by MSE quantification data shown in Figure 2

claim: Myelin basic protein (MBP) constitutes 18% (+/- 1% RSD) of the total myelin protein.
source: Myelin basic protein (MBP), periaxin (PRX) and tetraspanin-29 (CD9) constitute 18% (+/- 1% RSD), 15% (+/- 1%) and 1% (+/- 0.2%) of the total myelin protein, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by MSE quantification data shown in Figure 2

claim: Periaxin (PRX) constitutes 15% (+/- 1% RSD) of the total myelin protein.
source: Myelin basic protein (MBP), periaxin (PRX) and tetraspanin-29 (CD9) constitute 18% (+/- 1% RSD), 15% (+/- 1%) and 1% (+/- 0.2%) of the total myelin protein, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by MSE quantification data shown in Figure 2

claim: Tetraspanin-29 (CD9) constitutes 1% (+/- 0.2% RSD) of the total myelin protein.
source: Myelin basic protein (MBP), periaxin (PRX) and tetraspanin-29 (CD9) constitute 18% (+/- 1% RSD), 15% (+/- 1%) and 1% (+/- 0.2%) of the total myelin protein, respectively (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by MSE quantification data shown in Figure 2

claim: Known myelin proteins collectively constitute over 85% of the total myelin protein.
source: By MSE, known myelin proteins (Table 1) collectively constitute over 85% of the total myelin protein (Figure 2)
evidence: Supported by MSE quantification data shown in Figure 2

claim: Proteins not yet associated with myelin account for approximately 15% of the total myelin protein.
source: while proteins not yet associated with myelin account for the remaining 15% of the total myelin protein.
evidence: Inferred from the statement that known myelin proteins constitute over 85% of total myelin protein

claim: Significant mRNA abundance was detected for all 1046 transcripts for which an unambiguous unique gene identifier was found.
source: When comparing the proteome and transcriptome datasets, significant mRNA abundance was detected for all 1046 transcripts for which an unambiguous unique gene identifier was found (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3

claim: 126 transcripts displayed developmentally unchanged abundance levels with abundance changes below a threshold of 10% coefficient of variation.
source: 126 transcripts displayed developmentally unchanged abundance levels, that is, abundance changes below a threshold of 10% coefficient of variation (Figure 3B; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 3B

claim: 920 transcripts showed developmental abundance changes and were grouped into 5 clusters by fuzzy c-means clustering.
source: By fuzzy c-means clustering, those 920 transcripts that showed developmental abundance changes were grouped into 5 clusters (Figure 3A; Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The P6-UP cluster includes the highest proportion of known myelin proteins.
source: Among those, one cluster corresponds to an mRNA-abundance peak coinciding with an early phase of myelin biogenesis (cluster 'P6-UP'), which includes the highest proportion of known myelin proteins (Table 1)
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 3A and Table 1

claim: Proteins associated with the lipid metabolism are particularly enriched in the P6-UP and P18-UP clusters.
source: When analyzing the clusters of developmentally co-expressed transcripts (from Figure 3), proteins associated with the lipid metabolism were particularly enriched in the P6-UP and P18-UP clusters
evidence: Supported by GO-term analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: Proteins associated with the extracellular matrix (ECM) are over-represented in the U-shaped and Descending clusters.
source: while those associated with the extracellular matrix (ECM) were over-represented in the U-shaped and Descending clusters (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by GO-term analysis shown in Figure 4

claim: 31 myelin proteins are encoded by a proven neuropathy gene.
source: Indeed, 31 myelin proteins were identified to be encoded by a proven neuropathy gene (Table 2)
evidence: Supported by comparison with neuropathy disease genes shown in Table 2

claim: Prx-/- mice represent an established model of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4F.
source: Prx-/- mice represent an established model of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 4F (Guilbot et al., 2001; Berger et al., 2006; Marchesi et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Guilbot et al., 2001; Berger et al., 2006; Marchesi et al., 2010

claim: PRX was undetectable by MSE in Prx-/- myelin.
source: As expected, PRX was also undetectable by MSE in Prx-/- myelin, in which most of the total myelin protein was constituted by MPZ/P0 and MBP (Figure 5B; Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by MSE data shown in Figure 5B

claim: The abundance of dystrophin-related protein 2 (DRP2) is strongly reduced in Prx-/- myelin.
source: For example, the abundance of the periaxin-associated dystrophin-related protein 2 (DRP2) was strongly reduced in Prx-/- myelin, as previously shown by immunoblotting (Sherman et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE data and citation to Sherman et al., 2001

claim: The abundance of the monocarboxylate transporter MCT1 (SLC16A1) is significantly reduced in Prx-/- myelin.
source: Notably, the abundance of multiple other proteins was also significantly reduced in Prx-/- myelin, including the extracellular matrix protein laminin C1 (LAMC1; previously termed LAMB2), the laminin-associated protein nidogen (NID1), Ig-like cell adhesion molecules (CADM4, MAG), the desmosomal junction protein desmin (DES), cytoskeletal and cytoskeleton-associated proteins (EPB41L3, MAP1A, CORO1A, SPTBN1, various microtubular and intermediate filament monomers), the monocarboxylate transporter MCT1 (also termed SLC16A1) and the MCT1-associated (Philp et al., 2003) immunoglobulin superfamily protein basigin (BSG, also termed CD147).
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE differential analysis shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: The reduced abundance of MCT1 in Prx-/- myelin was confirmed by immunoblotting.
source: In this respect it was striking to find the abundance of MCT1 significantly reduced in peripheral myelin when PRX is lacking (Figure 5C), a result that we were able to confirm by immunoblotting (Figure 5E)
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 5E

claim: The reduced abundance of MCT1 in Prx-/- myelin was confirmed by immunolabeling of teased fiber preparations of sciatic nerves.
source: a result that we were able to confirm by immunoblotting (Figure 5E) and immunolabeling of teased fiber preparations of sciatic nerves (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5F

claim: Prx-/- mice display reduced axonal diameters.
source: Indeed, Prx-/- mice displayed reduced axonal diameters, a progressively reduced total number of axons and a considerable number of myelin whorls lacking a visible axon (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: Prx-/- mice display a progressively reduced total number of axons.
source: Indeed, Prx-/- mice displayed reduced axonal diameters, a progressively reduced total number of axons and a considerable number of myelin whorls lacking a visible axon (Figure 6)
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6

claim: Prx-/- mice display a considerable number of myelin whorls lacking a visible axon, indicative of impaired axonal integrity.
source: Indeed, Prx-/- mice displayed reduced axonal diameters, a progressively reduced total number of axons and a considerable number of myelin whorls lacking a visible axon (Figure 6), indicative of impaired axonal integrity (Edgar et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by histological analysis shown in Figure 6 and citation to Edgar et al., 2009

claim: The monocarboxylate transporter MCT1/SLC16A1 expressed by myelinating Schwann cells has been proposed to supply lactate or other glucose breakdown products to axons.
source: The monocarboxylate transporter MCT1/SLC16A1 expressed by myelinating oligodendrocytes (Lee et al., 2012; Fünfschilling et al., 2012) and Schwann cells (Domènech-Estévez et al., 2015; Morrison et al., 2015) has been proposed to supply lactate or other glucose breakdown products to axons, in which they may serve as substrate for the mitochondrial production of ATP (Morrison et al., 2013; Saab et al., 2013; Rinholm and Bergersen, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Domènech-Estévez et al., 2015; Morrison et al., 2015; Morrison et al., 2013; Saab et al., 2013; Rinholm and Bergersen, 2014

claim: Reduced expression of MCT1 in Slc16a1+/- mice impairs axonal integrity at least in the CNS.
source: Notably, reduced expression of MCT1 in Slc16a1+/- mice impairs axonal integrity at least in the CNS (Lee et al., 2012; Jha et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2012; Jha et al., 2020

claim: In Prx-/- myelin, Schmidt-Lanterman incisures (SLI) were largely undetectable by MAG immunolabeling.
source: Also note that, in Prx-/- myelin, SLI were largely undetectable by MAG immunolabeling.
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5F

claim: SLC16A1 co-distributes with MAG in Schmidt-Lanterman incisures (SLI) in control nerves but not in Prx-/- nerves.
source: Note that SLC16A1 co-distributes with MAG in Schmidt-Lanterman incisures (SLI) in control but not in Prx-/- nerves, in accordance with the reduced abundance of SLC16A1 in Prx-/- myelin (C–E).
evidence: Supported by immunolabeling data shown in Figure 5F

claim: The abundance of PLP/DM20 in myelin is unaltered in Prx-/- myelin.
source: For comparison, the abundance of the marker proteolipid protein (PLP/DM20) (Patzig et al., 2016a) and the periaxin-associated integrin beta-4 (ITGB4) (Raasakka et al., 2019) in myelin was unaltered in Prx-/- myelin.
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE differential analysis

claim: The abundance of integrin beta-4 (ITGB4) in myelin is unaltered in Prx-/- myelin.
source: For comparison, the abundance of the marker proteolipid protein (PLP/DM20) (Patzig et al., 2016a) and the periaxin-associated integrin beta-4 (ITGB4) (Raasakka et al., 2019) in myelin was unaltered in Prx-/- myelin.
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE differential analysis and citation to Raasakka et al., 2019

claim: Proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin include immune-related proteins (LGALS3, LYZ2, CTSD).
source: On the other hand, proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin included immune-related proteins (LGALS3, LYZ2, CTSD), cytoskeletal and cytoskeleton-associated proteins (CAPG, CORO1C, CNN3, several myosin heavy chain subunits), peroxisomal enzymes (CAT, HSD17B4, MDH1) and known myelin proteins (PLLP/plasmolipin, CRYAB, GJB1/CX32).
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE differential analysis shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: Proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin include cytoskeletal and cytoskeleton-associated proteins (CAPG, CORO1C, CNN3, several myosin heavy chain subunits).
source: On the other hand, proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin included immune-related proteins (LGALS3, LYZ2, CTSD), cytoskeletal and cytoskeleton-associated proteins (CAPG, CORO1C, CNN3, several myosin heavy chain subunits), peroxisomal enzymes (CAT, HSD17B4, MDH1) and known myelin proteins (PLLP/plasmolipin, CRYAB, GJB1/CX32).
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE differential analysis shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: Proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin include peroxisomal enzymes (CAT, HSD17B4, MDH1).
source: On the other hand, proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin included immune-related proteins (LGALS3, LYZ2, CTSD), cytoskeletal and cytoskeleton-associated proteins (CAPG, CORO1C, CNN3, several myosin heavy chain subunits), peroxisomal enzymes (CAT, HSD17B4, MDH1) and known myelin proteins (PLLP/plasmolipin, CRYAB, GJB1/CX32).
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE differential analysis shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: Proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin include known myelin proteins (PLLP/plasmolipin, CRYAB, GJB1/CX32).
source: On the other hand, proteins displaying the strongest abundance increase in Prx-/- myelin included immune-related proteins (LGALS3, LYZ2, CTSD), cytoskeletal and cytoskeleton-associated proteins (CAPG, CORO1C, CNN3, several myosin heavy chain subunits), peroxisomal enzymes (CAT, HSD17B4, MDH1) and known myelin proteins (PLLP/plasmolipin, CRYAB, GJB1/CX32).
evidence: Supported by DRE-UDMSE differential analysis shown in Figure 5C-D

claim: The current workflow of myelin proteome analysis is considerably less labor-intense compared to previous approaches using 2D-DIGE.
source: Indeed, compared to the previously used manual handling and in-gel digestion, the current workflow (schematically depicted in Figure 1A) is considerably less labor-intense, and automated FASP increases sample-to-sample reproducibility.
evidence: Comparison of workflows shown in Figure 1A

claim: Automated FASP increases sample-to-sample reproducibility compared to manual handling and in-gel digestion.
source: Indeed, compared to the previously used manual handling and in-gel digestion, the current workflow (schematically depicted in Figure 1A) is considerably less labor-intense, and automated FASP increases sample-to-sample reproducibility.
evidence: Based on comparison of methods

claim: The present workflow increases the efficacy of assessing the peripheral myelin proteome while shifting the main workload from manual sample preparation and gel-separation to automated acquisition and processing of data.
source: Together, the present workflow increases the efficacy of assessing the peripheral myelin proteome while shifting the main workload from manual sample preparation and gel-separation to automated acquisition and processing of data.
evidence: Based on comparison of workflows

claim: DRE-UDMSE is the data acquisition mode of choice most suitable for routine differential myelin proteome profiling.
source: We thus consider DRE-UDMSE as the data acquisition mode of choice most suitable for routine differential myelin proteome profiling (see below).
evidence: Based on evaluation of different data acquisition modes

claim: The number of proteins identified in myelin has approximately doubled compared to a previous approach.
source: This reflects both that the number of proteins identified in myelin has approximately doubled and that more neuropathy genes are known due to the common use of genome sequencing.
evidence: Comparison with previous study (Patzig et al., 2011)

claim: The number of proven neuropathy genes of which the encoded protein is mass spectrometrically identified in peripheral myelin has increased four-fold from eight to 32.
source: Compared to a previous approach (Patzig et al., 2011), the number of proven neuropathy genes of which the encoded protein is mass spectrometrically identified in peripheral myelin has increased four-fold from eight to 32 in the present study.
evidence: Comparison with previous study (Patzig et al., 2011) and current data in Table 2

claim: A subset of MPZ-mutations causes axonal CMT2I or CMT2J.
source: Indeed, a subset of MPZ-mutations causes axonal CMT2I or CMT2J (Gallardo et al., 2009; Leal et al., 2014; Tokuda et al., 2015; Duan et al., 2016; Fabrizi et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Gallardo et al., 2009; Leal et al., 2014; Tokuda et al., 2015; Duan et al., 2016; Fabrizi et al., 2018

claim: Axonal CMT2 caused by MPZ mutations probably reflects impaired axonal integrity as consequence of a mutation primarily affecting Schwann cells.
source: Indeed, a subset of MPZ-mutations causes axonal CMT2I or CMT2J (Gallardo et al., 2009; Leal et al., 2014; Tokuda et al., 2015; Duan et al., 2016; Fabrizi et al., 2018), probably reflecting impaired axonal integrity as consequence of a mutation primarily affecting Schwann cells.
evidence: Based on inference from cited literature

claim: The nuclear EGR2/KROX20 causative of demyelinating CMT1D has not been mass spectrometrically identified in myelin, reflecting that Schwann cell nuclei are efficiently removed during myelin purification.
source: We also note that the nuclear EGR2/KROX20 causative of demyelinating CMT1D has not been mass spectrometrically identified in myelin, reflecting that Schwann cell nuclei are efficiently removed during myelin purification.
evidence: Based on absence of detection and inference about purification efficiency

claim: Prx-/- mice display a progressive peripheral neuropathy including axon/myelin-units with abnormal myelin thickness, demyelination, tomaculae, onion bulbs, and reduced nerve conduction velocity.
source: Indeed, Prx-/- mice display a progressive peripheral neuropathy including axon/myelin-units with abnormal myelin thickness, demyelination, tomaculae, onion bulbs, reduced nerve conduction velocity (Gillespie et al., 2000)
evidence: Supported by citation to Gillespie et al., 2000

claim: Absence of Schmidt-Lanterman incisures (SLIs) and bands of Cajal in Prx-/- mice implies that the non-compact myelin compartments are impaired when PRX is lacking.
source: Absence of SLIs (Gillespie et al., 2000) and bands of Cajal (Court et al., 2004) imply that the non-compact myelin compartments are impaired when PRX is lacking.
evidence: Supported by citations to Gillespie et al., 2000 and Court et al., 2004

claim: The neuropathology in Prx-/- mice at the molecular level is more complex than previously anticipated.
source: Thus, the neuropathology in Prx-/- mice at the molecular level is more complex than previously anticipated.
evidence: Based on comprehensive differential proteome analysis revealing multiple altered proteins

claim: The reduced abundance of MCT1 in Prx-/- myelin may be a consequence of the impaired myelin ultrastructure.
source: Considering that MCT1 in Schwann cells mainly localizes to Schmidt Lanterman incisures (SLI) (Domènech-Estévez et al., 2015) and that SLI are largely absent from myelin when PRX is lacking (Gillespie et al., 2000), the reduced abundance of MCT1 in Prx-/- myelin may be a consequence of the impaired myelin ultrastructure.
evidence: Based on inference from cited literature and current data

claim: The diminishment of MCT1 may contribute to reduced axonal diameters or axonal loss in Prx-/- mice, probably in conjunction with other molecular or morphological defects.
source: Yet, considering that SLI are part of the cytosolic channels that may represent transport routes toward Schwann cell-dependent metabolic support of myelinated axons, the diminishment of MCT1 may contribute to reduced axonal diameters or axonal loss in Prx-/- mice, probably in conjunction with other molecular or morphological defects.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional consequences

claim: The in depth-analysis of proteins altered in neuropathy models can contribute to an improved understanding of nerve pathophysiology.
source: Together, the in depth-analysis of proteins altered in neuropathy models can contribute to an improved understanding of nerve pathophysiology.
evidence: Based on inference from the comprehensive analysis performed
